title: MNG/PNG chunk framing: length covers only data, overhead follows
summary: MNG chunks are 4-byte big-endian length, 4-byte type, length data bytes, 4-byte CRC; parsers read the 4-byte CRC and discard it before dispatch.
content: In MNG (and PNG), each chunk is framed as length(4) + type(4) + data(length) + CRC(4). The length field is the payload size only, not the chunk size, so a chunk with payload length N occupies N+12 stream bytes. The CRC is read into a local variable and discarded before the type-specific handler runs, so a malformed or dummy CRC does not prevent reaching the handler. Keep this in mind when constructing a minimal MNG: a short payload still requires the outer 12 framing bytes to be present.

title: MNG LOOP handler requires 5 payload bytes but checks only length > 0
summary: LOOP payload layout is 1-byte loop_level + 4-byte loop_iters at offset 1; a length check of >0 is insufficient and allows OOB read for lengths 1-4.
content: The MNG LOOP chunk payload is parsed as chunk[0] (loop_level) and mng_get_long(&chunk[1]) (loop_iters), so the minimum valid payload length is 5. The original handler guarded only `length > 0`, so declared lengths 1 through 4 pass the guard and then the 4-byte read at offset 1 runs past the buffer. For any format lesson: when a handler reads a one-byte field followed by a 4-byte field at offset one, the length validation must be derived from every field access, not from a coarse nonzero check.

title: MNG chunk buffer is allocated exactly to declared length
summary: The chunk payload allocation size equals the declared length, so reads within payload must be bounded by length; trailing CRC is outside that allocation.
content: During MNG parsing the chunk payload buffer is allocated based on the declared `length` field. Therefore a LOOP chunk with declared length 1 gets a 1-byte heap buffer, and mng_get_long(&chunk[1]) immediately reads from offsets 1 through 4, with the final byte beyond the allocation. The CRC bytes are read after the payload and are not part of that buffer. This makes the issue a true heap out-of-bounds read rather than an in-bounds malformed value.

title: MNG dispatch occurs by type after the signature; MHDR is not required to reach LOOP
summary: MNG chunk dispatch is driven by the 4-byte type after the 8-byte signature, so a LOOP chunk can be reached without first providing MHDR.
content: A minimal MNG file can start with the 8-byte MNG signature (0x8A 'MNG' CR LF 0x1A LF) and then directly place chunks; the reader walks chunks in order and dispatches on the 4-byte type. No MHDR is required for the LOOP branch, because the handler is selected by chunk type before any image-dimension context is checked. This is useful for targeted format testing: only the signature and the chunk of interest are needed to hit the specific parsing branch.

title: mng_get_long reads byte-by-byte; OOB manifests as READ of size 1 at the tail
summary: mng_get_long loads a 32-bit value with four single-byte reads, so an undersized buffer faults on the last byte read.
content: The helper used to fetch loop_iters performs four separate single-byte reads from the start pointer. When called with &chunk[1] on a 1-byte payload, it reads bytes at offsets 1, 2, 3, and 4 from the payload start; offset 4 is one past the heap allocation and is reported as a 1-byte heap-buffer-overflow READ. Recognizing this helper behavior is useful when reasoning about which exact offset will be out of bounds for a given declared chunk length.

title: MNG chunk construction trap: include 4 CRC bytes even if CRC is ignored
summary: The chunk parser consumes CRC bytes before dispatch, so a well-framed short chunk must include length+type+payload+CRC even when CRC value is dummy.
content: When hand-building a minimal MNG, each chunk must be framed as length(4) + type(4) + payload(length) + CRC(4). The parser reads and discards the CRC before calling the type-specific handler, so omitting those four bytes will desynchronize the chunk stream or cause an unrelated parse error. Use any dummy CRC value; validation is not performed for reaching the LOOP handler, but the framing bytes must still be present.

title: Overlong all-zero hex constants bypass truthy bounds checks
summary: When a hex parser only bounds-checks on nonzero nibbles, an all-zero digit tail walks backward past the value buffer.
content: The hex-integer token format is '0x' followed by hex digits; each pair of digits fills one byte of a fixed-size value buffer. In the vulnerable loop the bounds check is conditional on the parsed nibble being nonzero, so a long run of '0' digits skips the error return and the store `out[-(i/2)]` keeps moving before the buffer. Make the entire tail past the buffer zero digits, not just the final digit; a single nonzero digit near the threshold triggers the guard and stops the walk.

title: Backward pointer walks need outer-object redzone distance
summary: To turn an intra-object underflow into a sanitizer-visible crash, extend the zero tail until the access passes before the enclosing stack struct.
content: The vulnerable pointer starts at the last byte of a 128-byte union value (value.u8[127]); each two hex digits decrements the access index by one. A write one byte before that array is still inside the surrounding lexer/token object, and ASan will not flag intra-object access. Count the distance from the value buffer to the start of the outermost stack object and provide enough digits so `-(i/2)` reaches the redzone; in this layout roughly 336 all-zero digits were needed, while 335 stayed inside the object.

title: Zero-value read-modify-write is only visible with sanitizer instrumentation
summary: The OOB store is `|= 0`; optimized non-ASan builds can eliminate it, so validate against an instrumented parser build.
content: The unchecked write in this bug is a read-modify-write that ORs the zero nibble into memory; logically it leaves every byte unchanged. A non-sanitized optimized build may remove the store entirely, producing no crash even when the index is out of bounds. Use an ASan-instrumented build to observe the access, or target code paths that write nonzero data; otherwise absence of a crash does not prove the parser is safe.

title: NUL-terminated string harness requires exact byte layout
summary: Expression-string parser harnesses treat the last byte as a terminator; manual hex input must be one continuous buffer ending in 0x00 with no separators.
content: When feeding a token string like `0x...0` to a lexer harness, the input file must contain the exact bytes of the expression followed by a NUL terminator as the final byte. Builders that construct hex dumps easily omit the `00`, accidentally insert a space between prefix and digits, or start with `78` instead of `30 78`; the harness rejects or truncates such inputs. Verify the byte count and last byte before running.

title: Bounds guard placement with parity: two digits per output byte
summary: A hex parser that fills one byte from every two hexits advances its dangerous index every second digit, making parity and rounding critical to threshold calculations.
content: For this format each byte is composed from a pair of hex digits, so the OOB index is integer division of the digit counter by 2. The guard fires only after a byte boundary is crossed, so an even/odd digit count can change the minimal exploit length by one. When calculating the exact digit count, simulate the counter at the final digit rather than assuming '2*N digits' equals 'N bytes'.

title: Corrupted token fields can be a secondary crash path
summary: Backward zero-fill into a token structure first hits heap/string pointers; preserving them may keep cleanup safe, but zeroing type/lexer state can trigger asserts.
content: Before the underflow leaves the outer lexer object, the backward walk crosses the token's type, format, and string pointer fields. If those fields were initialized to NULL, freeing them is harmless; but if the walk goes far enough to zero the token type, the parser's post-condition assert (`token->type == INTEGER` or `ERROR`) fails. This means a properly sized all-zero tail can crash an assert-enabled build before it even reaches the stack redzone.

title: ELF DT_HASH: bucket index dereferenced before bounds guard
summary: In ELF SysV hash lookup, the symbol index from buckets[] can be passed to dynsym access before the nbucket guard, causing an OOB read.
content: DT_HASH starts with two 32-bit words: nbucket and nchain, followed by buckets[nbucket] and chains[nchain]. A common lookup implementation reads the starting symbol index from buckets[elf_hash(name) % nbucket] and uses it to index dynsym before testing `if (nbucket <= si) break;`. A bucket value that is outside the valid dynamic symbol array is therefore dereferenced first. When crafting ELF inputs, bucket entries that are slightly out of the symbol range can trigger the pre-guard dereference without needing an enormous index.

title: ELF DT_HASH chain array is sized by nchain but guarded by nbucket
summary: The DT_HASH chain walk checks chain indices against nbucket instead of nchain, so chain indices in [nchain, nbucket-1] read past the chain array.
content: The hash table layout is: nbucket at offset 0, nchain at offset 4, then the bucket and chain arrays. The chain array has nchain entries, but the traversal loop compares the next chain index against nbucket, not nchain. If nchain is smaller than nbucket, a chain value in the range [nchain, nbucket-1] passes the guard and still reads chains[si] out of bounds. This distinction between the two counts is a useful construction trap for malformed DT_HASH tables.

title: ELF dynamic-section ordering can skip DT_HASH validation
summary: DT_HASH size/chain validation is often conditional on the relative addresses of DT_SYMTAB and DT_HASH, and can be skipped by placing the symbol table before the hash table.
content: ELF dynamic tag processing sometimes validates the DT_HASH bucket/chain area only when the hash table's virtual address is below the symbol table's virtual address. If DT_SYMTAB is placed at a lower RVA than DT_HASH, the cross-check that would reject bad hash-table indices is skipped entirely. When constructing ELF test files, the relative RVA order of the dynamic tags is therefore part of the vulnerability surface.

title: ELF symnum_max from DT_STRTAB value ignores real dynsym size
summary: The symbol-index upper bound may be computed from DT_STRTAB.d_val (an address), so a large DT_STRTAB value lets bucket indices reach far OOB.
content: The dynamic symbol table has no explicit count; parsers may derive a maximum symbol index from DT_STRTAB.d_val divided by the Elf_Sym size rather than from the actual dynsym table size. For ELF32 the symbol entry size is 16, so a DT_STRTAB tag with a large d_val makes the `si >= symnum_max` guard almost useless. A moderate bucket or chain index can then pass the guard and read OOB from the small real dynsym table.

title: Minimal ET_DYN ELF with PT_DYNAMIC reaches DT_HASH lookup
summary: A small e_type=ET_DYN ELF with PT_LOAD and PT_DYNAMIC containing DT_HASH/DT_SYMTAB/DT_STRTAB is enough to reach the vulnerable hash-table symbol lookup.
content: To exercise DT_HASH parsing in an ELF loader or unpacker, an ET_DYN (e_type=3) file needs only an ELF header, one PT_LOAD that covers the file, one PT_DYNAMIC with tags for DT_HASH, DT_SYMTAB, DT_STRTAB, DT_STRSZ, and DT_NULL, and the referenced tables placed at matching file offsets. The dynamic segment must have filesz and memsz large enough to contain the tag area and be inside the PT_LOAD mapping. The lookup is triggered by the loader searching for a well-known symbol name such as JNI_OnLoad in the dynamic symbol table.

title: ELF SysV hash bucket selection is modulo nbucket
summary: The DT_HASH bucket index is elf_hash(name) % nbucket, so nbucket=1 always uses bucket[0] and multi-bucket tables can set every bucket to the same bad index.
content: ELF SysV hash maps a symbol name to buckets[elf_hash(name) % nbucket]. When nbucket is 1, every symbol lookup uses bucket[0], so a malformed value there is reached without knowing the exact hash of the searched name. For multi-bucket tables, setting every bucket to the same malformed index makes the trigger independent of which bucket the hash selects. This modulo relationship is a useful structural detail when targeting DT_HASH chain traversal.

title: MSL attribute values reach the text translator
summary: Every MSL element attribute value is passed through the generic text translator, so MSL is a direct injection surface for text-escape bugs.
content: In MSL, an element start tag causes each attribute value to be passed through the library's generic text translator, and the `print` element reaches this translator without needing a pre-existing image. This makes MSL a direct injection surface for text-escape handling, so simple scripts can exercise the translator. When looking for a translator bug, prefer the simplest MSL element that calls the translator directly.

title: MSL line splitting injects a space into XML attribute values
summary: MSL's script reader truncates each physical line and re-joins chunks with a literal space, so long attribute values cannot be treated as a single continuous token.
content: The MSL script reader reads input line-by-line through a bounded buffer; when a line is too long it is truncated and the parser appends a literal space before continuing. XML attribute normalization preserves this single inserted space, so a token split across lines is not byte-identical to the same token on one line. Length-sensitive inputs must account for that injected space when choosing the split point.

title: MVG text primitive reaches the same text translator
summary: MVG `text` primitives are a non-XML route into the same text-translation sink used by MSL attributes.
content: In MVG, the `text` drawing primitive is dispatched through the drawing engine and into the annotation/text path, which invokes the same generic text translator used by MSL attribute values. This gives a non-XML route to the same text-escape handling when the MVG format is the active decoder. A simple MVG text primitive is sufficient; no external image is needed.

title: `%[...]` key extraction writes NUL even for a missing key
summary: The `%[...]` text-escape branch writes a NUL terminator before lookup, so an overlong missing key still overflows.
content: In the text translator's `%[` branch, the sequence between `[` and `]` is copied into a fixed stack key buffer and then NUL-terminated before the key is looked up. The loop bound is off by one relative to the buffer size, so when the copied key length equals the buffer size the terminator write is one byte past the end. Even a missing or unterminated key triggers the write, so the key does not need to match any real attribute.

title: Raw git tag message separation: `\n\n` scan must not cross EOF
summary: A raw git tag's message section is parsed by searching for `\n\n`; an unterminated tail with no blank line makes that search run past the input buffer.
content:
In the raw git tag object layout, `object`, `type`, `tag`, and `tagger` are newline-terminated lines, and the message block is delimited by a blank line (`

`). The tag parser finds that delimiter with an unbounded `strstr` call on the remaining buffer. If the tag has a valid tagger line and the following tail contains no `

` and no NUL terminator, the search reads past the end of the object data. The trigger is therefore not a badly truncated header, but a structurally valid header followed by an unterminated, non-blank tail.

title: Git object header line: exactly 40 hex chars for the object OID
summary: Raw git object `object` line must be exactly 40 hex characters and a newline; hex-count off-by-one invalidates the entire parse.
content: The first line of a raw git tag is the object being tagged: `object ` followed by 40 hex chars and LF. The parser requires exactly 40 hex characters at the expected offset; using 39 or 47 characters causes OID parsing to reject the object before tag-specific fields are examined. Count the hex digits exactly, and place the LF immediately after the 40th hex character. This is a classic raw-object format constraint.

title: Git tagger line: valid signature is required to advance into the message area
summary: The `tagger` line must be a complete git signature (`Name <email> time tz\n`) so the parser stops exactly after LF; otherwise it bails before the message scan.
content: After the `tag` line, the raw git tag grammar expects a `tagger` line with a valid signature: a name, `<email>`, a timestamp, a timezone, and a trailing LF. The signature parser consumes through that LF and returns a pointer to the message block. If the line is malformed, parsing stops and the message-search code is never reached. For format construction, the tagger line must be syntactically valid and end with the LF, leaving the cursor on the byte immediately after it.

title: Raw git object dispatch: tree/commit parse failures do not prevent tag parse
summary: When a raw object buffer is tried against multiple object types, a failed tree/commit parse does not stop a subsequent tag parse attempt.
content: A raw git object contains a `type` line, but a multi-type parser may attempt parsing for each object type in turn. In this format family, tree and commit parsers can reject the same bytes while the tag parser still accepts enough of the header to reach the message block. Therefore a tag-object trigger only needs the tag header and tail; it need not be a valid tree or commit object. This is a useful trap when feeding raw git objects to a multi-type parser.

title: TIFF CIE Log photometric ignores ExtraSamples alpha in quantum selection
summary: LogL/LogLuv TIFFs with alpha (tag 338) create a sample-count mismatch in the decoder's quantum-selection switch.
content: When a TIFF uses PHOTOMETRIC_LOGL (32844) or PHOTOMETRIC_LOGLUV (32845), the code that picks the quantum type handles alpha for RGB/gray photometrics but not for these CIE Log types. It returns 1 sample for LogL and 3 for LogLuv regardless of ExtraSamples. If tag 338 marks an alpha sample, the image is marked as having matte, but the pixel import path never reads/initializes that alpha. This is the core structural trap for this format: alpha is declared in the IFD but dropped in the color-conversion path.

title: SGILOG LogL alpha requires SamplesPerPixel=1 with ExtraSamples declared separately
summary: Because the SGILOG codec rejects SamplesPerPixel != 1, a LogL+alpha edge case needs ExtraSamples while keeping spp=1.
content: The SGILOG compression handler enforces samples_per_pixel == 1 for CIE Log images. A generator that increments SamplesPerPixel to 2 for the alpha sample will be rejected before the interesting path is reached. To exercise the alpha edge case, leave SamplesPerPixel at 1 and add an ExtraSamples tag (338) with value 2 (unassociated alpha). This is malformed according to the TIFF spec, but it is accepted and lets the decoder set matte without changing the codec's sample-count check.

title: SGILOG float expansion writes 12 bytes/pixel regardless of declared BitsPerSample/sample count
summary: LogLuv/SGILOG decodes to CIE XYZ float triples; scanline buffers sized purely from IFD sample arithmetic under-size the row.
content: The SGILOG decoder's float format emits three 32-bit floats per pixel, i.e. 12 bytes per pixel. TIFFScanlineSize, however, is normally computed from the IFD's BitsPerSample and SamplesPerPixel. Any mismatch between the declared sample layout and the LogLuv photometric's logical 3-component output leaves a row buffer that is smaller than what the decoder writes. When constructing TIFFs, keep the declared SamplesPerPixel/BitsPerSample consistent with the SGILOG codec's fixed per-pixel output size.

title: TIFF Compression tag must be SGILOG (34676) to select the LogL/LogLuv float decoder
summary: The dangerous CIE Log behavior is tied to COMPRESSION_SGILOG, not just the Photometric tag.
content: Setting PHOTOMETRIC_LOGL or LOGLUV without Compression=34676 does not engage the SGILOG codec and misses the interesting decode path. In the TIFF IFD, tag 259 must contain 34676 (0x8774) while tag 262 contains 32844/32845. The Photometric/Compression pair is a precondition; keep both tags consistent or the file falls through to a different reader path.

title: 16-bit tag values are stored little-endian in II TIFF IFD entries
summary: Hand-built TIFF IFDs require little-endian encoding for multi-byte tag values such as Photometric 32844.
content: In an 'II' little-endian TIFF, an IFD value field is a 4-byte little-endian integer. PhotometricInterpretation 32844 is therefore encoded as 4c 80 00 00. Getting this byte order wrong silently changes the photometric to an unintended value (for example 0x4c80 = 19584), making the file hit a completely different decoder path. This is an easy construction trap when patching an existing TIFF seed.

title: Confirm which coder the harness actually compiles before choosing MSL/MVG
summary: A coder-driven fuzzer is built with a single coder baked in; an MSL payload is inert if the binary is an MVG coder, so verify reachability first.
content: The same library has several format coders that call the text translator, but a coder-fuzzer target only exercises the read path of the coder it was compiled with. Running a quick probe with the intended MSL document showed no effect because the loaded coder was MVG. Determine the compiled coder from the build setup, or test both formats early, before spending effort on a full-length payload.

title: LABEL coder text comes from the filename, not the file body
summary: The LABEL format makes the filename itself the rendered text, so it is only a viable format-string route when the filename is user-controlled.
content: In the LABEL format, the image body is ignored and the label text is taken from the image filename, then passed through the text translator. A fuzzer that always sets the filename to the coder name plus a colon makes the label text fixed and useless for reaching a format-string bug. Do not select LABEL unless you can prove the filename or prefix is attacker-controlled.

title: MVG path subpaths: each M starts a new open subpath
summary: Multiple M commands inside one MVG path create independent subpaths that each add extra path_info entries.
content: In MVG, a path primitive can hold several M commands, and each M starts a new subpath within the same PathPrimitive rather than being flattened. When converting such a path to the internal PathInfo array, every unclosed subpath (one not ended with Z) adds ghost-line entries after its points. This makes multi-subpath open paths behave very differently from a single polyline and is a core source of length-miscount vulnerabilities.

title: MVG tokenizer quoting affects path delivery
summary: Path data with spaces is tokenized unless quoted, so multi-subpath paths must be kept as one token.
content: MVG reads the path argument with a drawing tokenizer. If path data contains spaces and is not quoted, tokenization can split the path into separate commands, so an M ... M ... path may not reach the path tracer as a single path. When testing MVG path parsing, keep the whole path in one quoted argument or remove whitespace so the subpath structure survives tokenization.

title: First subpath must pass coordinates>1 guard
summary: The MVG polygon converter skips paths whose first subpath has only one point.
content: Vector rendering skips polygon conversion when the first primitive's coordinates field is 1 or less. Therefore a path that begins with a single-point M will not reach the vulnerable conversion, no matter how many later subpaths are present. The first subpath must contain at least two points to pass the guard; later subpaths may be degenerate one-point open subpaths and still contribute to the write count.

title: PathInfo capacity vs open-subpath write count
summary: The path_info allocation assumes closed polylines; open subpaths add extra ghost-line writes that can exceed capacity.
content: The PathInfo buffer is sized as 2*i+3 records, where i is the primitive_info element count. During conversion, each point writes one normal entry, each open subpath writes an extra ghost-line pair, and an EndCode terminator is written at the end. A path with several small open subpaths can require points + 2*open_subpaths + 1 records, which exceeds the allocation when enough small open subpaths are present. The excess write appears when assigning the code field of a PathInfo entry.

title: Fill rendering reaches polygon conversion
summary: Stroke-only MVG paths may be handled by a different path and skip the vulnerable conversion.
content: In MVG vector drawing, stroke-only rendering can expand the path into a separate geometry before the vulnerable conversion code runs, while fill rendering sends the original path into DrawPolygonPrimitive. To keep exercising the path-conversion logic, configure the path as a filled primitive rather than relying only on stroke. This avoids spending fuzzing iterations on a code path that does not reach the target conversion.

title: Small overflows are hidden by allocator rounding
summary: A one-entry PathInfo overflow may not crash, so reliable MVG triggers need enough open subpaths to cross allocated slack.
content: The PathInfo allocation is rounded up by heap allocators, so a single PathInfo write past the nominal capacity often lands in slack and produces no crash or ASan report. A reliable reproducer needs several trailing one-point open subpaths so the write count exceeds the capacity by enough entries to hit a redzone. When developing MVG path triggers, over-saturating the capacity is more dependable than stopping at the mathematical threshold.

title: MVG ellipse command: geometry values are strtod text fields
summary: MVG primitive commands accept arbitrary floating-point text; huge numeric literals are only checked later.
content: An MVG ellipse primitive is written as ellipse cx,cy rx,ry start_deg,end_deg, where all fields are parsed by strtod. The parser accepts enormously large decimal exponents and does not reject them at the tokenizer stage. Validation happens later inside primitive construction, so a format-level test must know which later arithmetic checks dominate.

title: Ellipse preallocation uses hypot(radii), not arc span
summary: The parser estimates primitive-array size from ellipse radii; it does not account for the angle span, so huge start/end degrees bypass the pre-check.
content: For the ellipse primitive, the parser's initial points_length estimate is computed from the hypot of the radius values plus fixed constants. Very large radii can make that estimate overflow to infinity and trigger an arithmetic exception before the ellipse tracing routine is reached. A huge arc-angle span, however, is not part of that estimate, so it reaches the ellipse trace routine while the initial allocation remains small. Use an extreme angle value rather than an extreme radius when trying to exercise angle-based arithmetic.

title: TraceEllipse count formula differs from the parser estimate
summary: The actual primitive count is derived from the arc angle divided by the angular step, so it can be much larger than the parser's radius-based preallocation.
content: TraceEllipse computes a needed-element count from the difference of the start/end angles divided by the generated step. In the MVG renderer this count is the authoritative allocation size, not the parser's earlier estimate. A small radius gives a step around MagickPI divided by 8, making the count roughly the angle span in degrees divided by 22.5. This lets a huge end-degree field drive the count above the parser's estimate and out of the allocated PrimitiveInfo array.

title: Floating-to-size_t wrap creates small allocation with huge write loop
summary: When the computed quotient exceeds 2^64, casting to size_t can yield a small number on x86-64, so the allocation appears small while the loop count stays huge.
content: The needed count is computed as 1 plus a cast of a floating-point ceil result to size_t. On x86-64, an out-of-range double that is cast to size_t truncates to its low bits. An angle-span divided by step quotient just below 2^63 tends to cast to 2^63 and fail as a gigantic allocation request, whereas a quotient in the 2^64 band can cast to a small positive value. That band is the useful one for constructing a heap overwrite: the renderer allocates for the wrapped small count but the subsequent drawing loop continues for the unwrapped number of iterations.

title: Allocation failure can leave a NULL primitive-info pointer
summary: When realloc fails, the renderer can store the requested count, set the pointer to NULL, and return success, so later writes go to address zero.
content: The ellipse trace routine asks PrimitiveInfoRealloc for the computed count; if that allocation fails, the helper can leave a NULL primitive-info pointer and a bogus large allocation count before returning success. The caller then treats the NULL pointer as valid and starts writing trace records, causing a crash. For a stable crash without an out-of-bounds write, this is an alternative trigger, but for a controlled overwrite the pre-wrap huge-count path is less useful.

title: MNG/PNG chunk envelope: length, type, data, CRC
summary: MNG chunks reuse the PNG chunk layout: 4-byte big-endian length, 4-byte type, data, then 4-byte CRC; length counts only the data.
content: MNG chunks are composed of a 4-byte big-endian length, a 4-byte type, the data field, and a 4-byte CRC. The length covers only the data field, so a chunk with declared length 1 has exactly one data byte even though the type and CRC still follow it. When crafting minimal MNG inputs, include the 4-byte CRC placeholder after the data; the parser consumes it during chunk iteration even though it does not validate it.

title: MNG signature bytes
summary: MNG files must start with the 8-byte signature 0x8a 'MNG' CR LF 0x1a LF to be dispatched to the MNG reader.
content: The MNG container signature is 8a 4d 4e 47 0d 0a 1a 0a, i.e. 0x8a, the literal ASCII bytes 'MNG', carriage return, line feed, 0x1a, and line feed. The decoder requires this exact prefix to enter the MNG chunk loop; any other first bytes are not treated as MNG. Use this signature as the first bytes of every minimal MNG container.

title: MNG LOOP chunk data layout requires 5 bytes
summary: The LOOP payload is one level byte followed by a 4-byte big-endian iteration count, so its declared length must be at least 5.
content: The MNG LOOP chunk payload is laid out as byte 0 containing the loop level and bytes 1..4 containing the loop iteration count in big-endian order. The chunk dispatcher only tests that the declared length is greater than zero before reading these fields, so a payload of 1..4 bytes passes the guard but causes the 4-byte read at offset 1 to run past the chunk buffer. When probing chunk parsers, verify that every multi-byte field read from a chunk offset is covered by the declared length, not merely by a positive-length check.

title: Short LOOP payload over-reads at offset 1
summary: A LOOP chunk with declared length 1..4 reads a big-endian 32-bit field starting at payload offset 1, producing a heap-buffer-overflow.
content: For a LOOP payload of N bytes where 1 <= N <= 4, the chunk buffer is allocated with N bytes, but the handler reads chunk[0] and then 4 bytes starting at chunk[1]. The final byte of that read is at offset N, exactly one past the end of the allocation when the declared length equals N. This means any LOOP chunk carrying only 1..4 data bytes is enough to trigger the over-read; no additional MNG chunks are required before it.

title: MNG chunk loop is reachable without MHDR
summary: The MNG chunk loop starts right after the signature; LOOP can be the first chunk and no MEND terminator is needed to trigger a crash.
content: The parser begins reading chunks immediately after the 8-byte MNG signature, without requiring an MHDR chunk first or a MEND chunk to reach the LOOP handler. This allows a minimal container to be just the signature followed by one malformed chunk. For inputs that crash during chunk processing, adding header or terminator chunks is unnecessary and only changes the byte offset before the fault.

title: 1-and-0 padding: the 0x01 marker must precede the zero run
summary: A valid 1-and-0 padded buffer needs at least one 0x01 marker before trailing zero bytes; a zero-only buffer is structurally invalid and crashes the backward unpadder.
content: In the 1-and-0 padding format, the input is a raw byte buffer with no magic or header; the structure is: original bytes, then a 0x01 marker, then zero bytes. The reference unpadder walks backward over trailing 0x00 bytes and expects to hit the 0x01 marker before reaching the start. If the buffer has no marker, the backward scan crosses the buffer start and dereferences an out-of-bounds offset. When constructing inputs for this format, enforce that the trailing zero run is shorter than the buffer length so the 0x01 marker stays in bounds.

title: 1-and-0 padding: backward scans need a signed or bounded index
summary: Parsing 1-and-0 padding by decrementing an unsigned length-based offset from the end is unsafe unless the zero run is bounded.
content: The 1-and-0 format has no end-of-buffer sentinel; the parser receives a separate length and must rely on the 0x01 marker to stop the backward zero-run scan. Because the scan offset starts at the last byte and decrements while bytes are zero, a markerless zero-filled buffer drives the offset below zero and wraps to a huge value. A format-construction rule that prevents this is to make the trailing zero run length strictly less than the buffer length, leaving at least the marker byte in bounds. This keeps the backward walk within the allocated buffer and preserves the 1-and-0 structure.

title: magic(5) regex rules are anchored at a fixed byte offset
summary: A FILE_REGEX rule is applied at the rule's offset, so the matching text must begin at that offset.
content: The magic database row format is `offset type test message`. For `type` = `regex`, the magic rule engine passes the buffer position at that `offset` to regexec, so a caret in the test pattern anchors to that offset rather than to the start of the whole file. The default c-lang rule is `0 regex ^#include C source text`: offset 0, so the first bytes of the input must contain the preprocessor token `#include`. Other regex entries in the database can have different offsets or length constraints, so choosing an offset-0 rule avoids padding calculations.

title: Hex-integer literal: all-zero digit run bypasses the per-nibble length check
summary: In a 0x-prefixed hex literal, a parser that enforces the value-buffer limit only for non-zero digits lets an all-zero run underflow the buffer.
content: The token format is `0x` followed by ASCII hex digits. The parser accumulates nibbles backwards into a fixed `value` buffer and has a bounds check that is evaluated only when the current nibble is nonzero. With all `0` digits, every nibble skips the check and the loop continues past the buffer limit. For format testing, the all-zero overlong literal is the critical edge case: a single nonzero digit at the boundary would hit the length check before the out-of-bounds access.

title: Backward write index: compute the redzone boundary from the buffer end to the enclosing object start
summary: To make an underflow visible to ASan, the backward index must cross the start of the containing lexer object, not just the start of the value buffer.
content: The value buffer is a 128-byte union inside a token struct embedded in the lexer; `out` points to its last byte. The access is at `object_start + value_offset + 127 - (i/2)`. The first access outside the stack object occurs when `i/2` exceeds `value_offset + 127`, so use struct field offsets rather than buffer size alone to choose the literal length. Smaller overlong literals may corrupt only padding or still-intra-object fields and will not trigger a stack-buffer-underflow report.

title: Trailing NUL terminator is part of the input contract for textual lexer test cases
summary: Raw input files for lexer harnesses must end with 0x00; hex-encoded digit strings that omit the terminator are rejected before parsing.
content: When constructing raw input for a string lexer, append an explicit `0x00` byte after the last character. If the file is produced by hex-encoding ASCII digits, it is easy to end with `0x30` (the last '0') instead of `0x00`; the harness entry guard rejects files whose final byte is not NUL. Keep the input free of newline bytes, since newline terminates the token and prevents the long literal from being parsed as one token.

title: OOB read-modify-write with OR 0 is observable only under a sanitizer
summary: An out-of-bounds `|= 0` leaves memory unchanged, so an uninstrumented run can exit clean despite the bug; validate with ASan.
content: The vulnerable step is `out[-(i/2)] |= nibble`. When all hex digits are `0`, the OR writes no new value, so ordinary builds show no crash or data corruption even though the access is out of bounds. The access is still an OOB read, and ASan reports it as a stack-buffer-underflow. For confirmation, run the overlong all-zero literal under a sanitizer build; do not infer absence of the bug from a clean exit code in a non-ASan binary.

title: OVN expression operand forms: literal braces vs named set references
summary: In OVN expression strings, an operand set is parsed differently depending on whether it is an inline `{...}` literal or a `$`/`@` reference to an address set/port group.
content: The OVN expression grammar has two operand forms for value sets: an inline curly-brace list and a symbolic reference to an address set or port group. The parser marks literal brace constants with an `in_curlies` flag, but named references do not set that flag even when the referenced set is empty. When crafting expressions, the operand syntax matters: an empty literal set is rejected early for relational operators, while an empty named reference reaches deeper evaluation logic. This parser distinction is a key structural trap for the comparison path.

title: OVN comparison evaluation: relational ops read values[0] before the empty-set guard
summary: For `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on a named empty value set, the evaluator reads `cs->values[0]` before checking `cs->n_values`, causing an invalid access.
content: Inside the OVN comparison construction routine, the masked value is read from `cs->values[0]` for relational operators before the code checks whether `cs->n_values == 0`. An empty named address set or port group has `n_values == 0` but still reaches this path because it is not a literal brace set. The `==` and `!=` operators are safe because they check `n_values` first. A minimal expression for this class uses an ordinal, type-compatible field such as an IPv4 address field together with one of `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and an empty named set reference.

title: PhaseOne strip container header
summary: The PhaseOne raw format starts with a fixed image header plus a strip table of row-selector records.
content: A PhaseOne raw container is parsed as five little-endian u32 header fields (width, height, type, cpp, isCFA), followed by a u32 strip count, then that many strip records. Each strip record is an explicit destination row index n, a u32 byte length, and the strip payload. The header fields are validated before the strip records, so an input must satisfy the width/height/type/cpp and strip-count constraints first.

title: Strip n is a row selector, not a sequence
summary: The per-strip n field chooses the destination row, so duplicates leave other rows uninitialized.
content: In PhaseOne's strip table, the first u32 of each strip record is the row index for that strip's decompressed data. The decoder writes to (width, n), not to the next available row, so a duplicate n causes some rows to be skipped entirely. This is the key construction trap: keep every n within [0, height) but use repeated selectors to leave at least one row without a write. Memory-initialization checks then fail when that uninitialized row is consumed.

title: Out-of-range n throws; duplicate n triggers uninitialized state
summary: An out-of-bounds row selector is caught cleanly, while an in-bounds duplicate reaches the vulnerable write pattern.
content: PhaseOne row lookup performs bounds checking on n and raises a decoder exception for out-of-range values. The surrounding harness catches that exception and reports a clean decode error, so an invalid row index does not produce the target crash. Instead, the useful input is one where all n values are in-bounds but not unique, because that passes validation yet creates rows that are never initialized. The crash then comes only when the image is checked for initialized memory, not from the row access itself.

title: NSH md2 hex field scan cap vs decoded byte length
summary: The `md2=0x...` field in the ODP action string is scanned with a 511-char limit, but decoded bytes are half that, so the fixed 248-byte stack buffer can be exceeded.
content: In the ODP action grammar, NSH md2 payload is written as `md2=0x` followed by hex digits. The parser scans at most 511 hex characters, then converts pairs to bytes: the decoded length is at most about 255 bytes. The receiver keeps this data in a fixed 248-byte stack metadata array, so the scan cap does not protect the array from overflow; 255 bytes already exceeds it. Keep in mind that a textual hex limit is not a byte-length limit when auditing this format.

title: NSH md2 alignment padding is added to the copied length
summary: NSH md2 parsing pads the decoded payload to a 4-byte boundary and uses the padded size as the authoritative metadata length, making the effective length larger than the hex field's decoded bytes.
content: After decoding the `md2` hex field, the parser computes `padding = (4 - mdlen % 4) % 4` and prepends that many zero bytes. The resulting metadata length is `mdlen + padding`, and this padded length is what later code passes to the attribute/copy routine. Therefore a decoded length of 248 can become 248, but 249 becomes 252, and 255 becomes 256; the padding can push an already-oversized field further beyond the stack buffer. When constructing or auditing this grammar, always account for the final aligned length, not just the decoded hex length.

title: Temporary buffer reallocation invalidates the original stack metadata array
summary: The ODP action parser seeds its temporary byte buffer with a local stack array, and any prepend-zero operation can force the buffer to move, after which the local array no longer holds the complete data.
content: The ODP action parser initializes its temporary byte buffer on a stack array of fixed size, then appends decoded `md2` bytes. A subsequent prepend-zero operation for the NSH alignment padding requests headroom that does not exist, so the buffer moves or copies its contents elsewhere. If later parser code still treats the original stack array as the source of metadata, it reads stale or out-of-bounds stack bytes. For this format, the critical trigger is any md2 field long enough that appended data plus padding forces the temporary buffer to leave its initial stack backing store.

title: ODP action string must be NUL-terminated and newline-free
summary: The ODP action text harness consumes a single null-terminated string and rejects newlines, so action strings like `push_nsh(...)` must end at the NUL without a trailing newline.
content: The harness for ODP action parsing reads the input as a null-terminated string, and the action grammar stops at the closing parenthesis; a newline byte is not part of the accepted syntax and will break the parse. This means when constructing an action string for this format, terminate it with NUL and omit any line terminator. The size constraint is minimal, but the exact terminator requirement matters because the parser does not strip whitespace.

title: ODP push_nsh md2 hex overflow: ofpbuf expansion masks the write, not the read
summary: In ODP push_nsh parsing, a hex md2 payload longer than 248 bytes makes ofpbuf reallocate to heap; the later attribute marshalling reads from the original 248-byte stack array.
content: The ODP push_nsh action takes mdtype=2 and an md2 payload as a 0x-prefixed hex string. The parser decodes this hex into an ofpbuf that is initially backed by a 248-byte stack metadata array (NSH_CTX_HDRS_MAX_LEN). When the decoded length exceeds 248, ofpbuf's stub writer expands to heap memory, so there is no stack write overflow at the decode step. The overflow is instead a read: after the action is parsed, the NSH key marshalling routine serializes md_size bytes from the original stack metadata array, not from the expanded buffer. The format trap is that a textually valid md2 payload can exceed the container's stated 248-byte metadata limit and still parse.

title: NSH md2 length rounding and uint8_t wrap create a 4-byte OOB window
summary: The vulnerable md2 length window is just over 248 bytes because the rounded length is stored as uint8_t and wraps at 256.
content: NSH metadata length is derived from the decoded md2 payload and rounded up to a 4-byte alignment before serialization. The rounded value is kept in a uint8_t: decoded lengths 249..252 round to 252, which reads 4 bytes past the 248-byte metadata array. At decoded length 253, the rounded value wraps to 0 and the over-read disappears. So the format's dangerous input window is a narrow band immediately above the 248-byte context-header maximum, not an arbitrary huge payload; fuzzing should include lengths 249, 250, 251, and 252 specifically.

title: Parser and formatter disagree on NSH md2 maximum
summary: ODP push_nsh has one path that rejects mdlen > 248 and another that does not, making the over-limit form parseable.
content: In the ODP push_nsh action grammar, the md2 field's hex characters are consumed with a bounded 511-character scan, so raw payloads are capped at 255 decoded bytes; the formatter/validator path rejects decoded lengths over 248 with an error, but the action-parser path does not apply that same bound. This means an input can contain an md2 payload that would never be produced by a valid round-trip of the format, yet is accepted by the parser and leads to the out-of-bounds read. A format parser and emitter that share this grammar must enforce the same structural limits, here the 248-byte NSH context header maximum, before using a length field.

title: Git tag object message separator controls OOB scan
summary: After a valid tagger line, the Git tag message block is scanned with unbounded strstr for '\n\n'; absence of that separator and of a NUL triggers an OOB read.
content:
A Git raw tag object is a sequence of text headers: object <40-hex>
, type <type>
, tag <name>
, tagger <signature>
, then a message block. The parser separates the message from the headers by searching for a literal two-byte '

' sequence. If the remaining message bytes contain no '

' and the input is not NUL-terminated, the unbounded strstr search continues past the logical end of the buffer. Message content must either include the separator or be absent; a single non-newline byte after the tagger line is enough to reach the unbounded scan.

title: Git object id field must be exactly 40 hex characters
summary: In the object header, Git's oid parser requires exactly 40 hex chars plus a newline; off-by-one hex counts abort before the tag message scan.
content: The 'object' line starts with the literal 'object ' followed by a 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 and then '\n'. The parser's oid reader consumes exactly 40 hex digits and immediately requires the newline at that position. Using 39 or 41 hex characters makes the line fail to parse, so the tag parser returns before the vulnerable message lookup. Keep the oid length exact and the newline at offset 47 from the start of the line.

title: Tagger signature must parse completely for message block to run
summary: A Git tag's tagger line must be a valid signature (Name <email> timestamp tz) because malformed signatures make the parser fail before scanning the message.
content: After the tag name line, the tagger line must be a complete git signature: display name, space, '<email>', space, Unix timestamp, space, timezone offset, then newline. The parser advances through this signature and leaves the buffer pointing after the terminating newline. If the signature is malformed, tagger parsing returns an error and the message-block strstr is never executed. Use a valid signature with all four components and a trailing newline.

title: NUL-termination behavior of the fuzzer driver changes exploitability
summary: The unbounded strstr OOB in Git tag parsing only manifests when the raw input buffer is not NUL-terminated; drivers that append a NUL mask the bug.
content: The tag message scan relies on the absence of both '\n\n' and a NUL terminator. If the fuzzing harness appends a zero byte after the input, strstr stops at that in-bounds NUL and the read stays within the allocation. When reproducing against a harness that passes raw bytes without a terminator, the same input triggers a heap-buffer-overflow read. Verify whether the target runner appends a terminator before judging an input as non-crashing.

title: Raw object harness tries all four Git object types
summary: An object fuzzer that loops over blob/tree/commit/tag will still run tag parsing after a blob parse succeeds, so design tag inputs to parse as tag.
content: The raw Git object harness attempts to parse the input as each of the four object types. Because a blob is any byte sequence, a tag trigger will 'succeed' as a blob first, but the harness continues to the later type parsers rather than stopping. The tag-specific parse can therefore still be reached by the same bytes. To hit the tag message logic, the input must additionally be a structurally valid tag header (object, type, tag, tagger), not just valid as a blob.

title: Git commit object: valid 'tree' header is required before author parsing
summary: The commit parser must see `tree <40 hex>\n` before it enters the author-line loop; malformed tree lines abort early.
content: A raw Git commit object starts with `tree ` followed by exactly 40 hexadecimal characters and a newline. The parser uses this line to locate the start of header fields, and if the tree line is absent or the OID is too short/long it bails before any author-prefix boundary check. For fuzzing the author-detection path, the prefix must therefore always be preceded by a structurally valid tree line; the tree OID itself need not refer to an existing object, 40 hex chars are enough to pass the parser.

title: Git commit object: exact trailing 'author ' triggers one-byte OOB read
summary: Ending a commit buffer with exactly `author ` (7 bytes, no newline/NUL) makes the author-prefix loop read one byte past the buffer.
content: The author-detection loop checks that at least 7 bytes remain and then compares with the literal `author `. If the remaining bytes are exactly `author ` and the input has no terminator, the comparison reads the following byte while testing whether the literal ended. This boundary condition is specific to the commit header field layout: `author ` followed by any in-buffer byte, even a newline or `x`, does not produce the same over-read. Keep the trailing bytes at exactly the prefix length.

title: Git commit object: author field layout for multi-author test cases
summary: A valid author signature line is `author Name <email> timestamp +offset\n`; use one before a truncated second author so parsing reaches the next loop.
content: When the intended trigger is a second `author ` tail, the first author line must be complete: `author `, name, ` <email> `, timestamp, space, UTC offset with sign, newline. For example `author A <a@b> 0 +0000\n` is accepted. If this first signature is malformed, the parser rejects the commit before the loop can inspect the next author prefix, so the tail is never reached. This layout also provides useful padding if you need to adjust total input size.

title: Git commit object: raw-buffer input channel must not NUL-terminate
summary: The one-byte over-read disappears if the harness appends a NUL after the commit bytes; use raw-byte fuzzer inputs.
content: Some file-reading utilities allocate `len+1` and write a NUL at `data[len]`, so a commit ending in `author ` is followed by an in-bounds NUL and the prefix comparison stops cleanly. The bug only manifests when the fuzzer passes the raw commit object bytes with no implicit terminator and the byte after `author ` is outside the object. Always check whether the target input path adds a terminator before declaring a boundary test to be a no-op.

title: Git commit object: pad input to allocation capacity to catch 1-byte redzone over-read
summary: A one-byte OOB read is only observed by ASan if the byte after the commit buffer sits in a redzone; choose the total length to match the engine's buffer capacity.
content: If the fuzzer engine allocates the input in power-of-two-sized chunks, a 1-byte over-read at `buffer[size]` is silent unless `size` equals the allocation capacity. You can pad the Git commit object with a longer author name/email or additional valid header content before the final 7-byte `author ` tail to land exactly on that boundary. This is a common construction trap: the commit format allows arbitrary-length names/emails, making it easy to tune the total byte length without changing the semantics.

title: ELF DT_HASH: chain bound is checked after use, and against nbucket not nchain
summary: The ELF hash-table chain walk dereferences the next index before validating it, so a single crafted chain value triggers an out-of-bounds read.
content: In an ELF DT_HASH table, the first 32-bit word is nbucket, the second is nchain, then come bucket[nbucket] and chain[nchain]. The symbol lookup loop pulls the next index from the chain array and uses it before the guard `if (nbucket <= si) break` runs. That guard is also against nbucket even though the chain array has only nchain entries, so any index in [nchain, nbucket) passes the guard but is already out of bounds for chain[]. To reach the OOB read, make nchain smaller than nbucket and give the first bucket a chain index in that gap or far beyond the buffer.

title: ELF dynamic-tag order: place DT_HASH after DT_SYMTAB to skip index validation
summary: Validation of DT_HASH chain indices is only done when the hash table lies before the symbol table, so reordering the two dynamic tags bypasses it.
content: Packers that parse PT_DYNAMIC often condition a chain-index maximum check on the relative virtual addresses of DT_HASH and DT_SYMTAB. If v_hsh < v_sym, they require the longest chain to fit inside the dynsym table; if v_hsh > v_sym, that validation branch is skipped. Therefore, when crafting an ELF with a malformed DT_HASH, place the hash table at a higher virtual address than the symbol table. The dynamic array must still contain both tags and end with DT_NULL.

title: ELF symnum_max from DT_STRTAB is a VA-derived number, not the dynsym count
summary: The symbol-name lookup guard uses DT_STRTAB's value/16, so a high string-table VA makes the OOB symbol index look valid.
content: When the lookup resolves a symbol name, the maximum symbol index is derived from the DT_STRTAB tag's d_val divided by the ELF32 symbol size (16), not from the actual number of dynamic symbols. If DT_STRTAB points at a large virtual address, the resulting symnum_max is enormous, so the guard `si < symnum_max` accepts any practical OOB index. The subsequent dynsym[si] access is then an out-of-bounds read even though the index is far beyond the real symbol table.

title: Poison all ELF hash buckets so the name lookup cannot dodge the OOB index
summary: Filling every DT_HASH bucket with the same large index makes the trigger independent of which bucket the target symbol name hashes to.
content: ELF's System V hash selects a bucket by `elf_hash(name) % nbucket`. If only one bucket is malicious, the symbol name actually looked up must hash to exactly that bucket. To avoid depending on the name, set every bucket to the same poisoned chain/bucket index; whichever bucket is selected, the lookup immediately follows the bad index. With nbucket=2, this means both 32-bit bucket values are large.

title: Minimal ET_DYN must pass harness size and program-header sanity checks
summary: A minimum valid ELF32 ET_DYN with PT_LOAD and PT_DYNAMIC is required before the dynamic hash-table path is reachable.
content: The harness rejects tiny inputs with "file is too small" before format dispatch, so the file must be at least around 200 bytes. The needed structure is: ELF32 header with e_type=3 (ET_DYN), a PT_LOAD program header covering the file, and a PT_DYNAMIC program header whose offset points to the dynamic array. The dynamic array must include DT_HASH, DT_SYMTAB, DT_STRTAB, DT_STRSZ and a terminating DT_NULL. Keeping PT_LOAD's p_filesz/p_memsz equal to the file length avoids earlier sanity rejections.

title: Unpack/test mode can reach the ELF DT_HASH lookup on ET_DYN
summary: The vulnerable name lookup is reachable from decompression/test handling of ET_DYN, not only from compression, because the same dynamic-section setup runs.
content: For an ET_DYN input, the decompression/test path runs the same PT_DYNAMIC and elf_lookup setup as compression before checking the pack header. This means a malformed DT_HASH can be triggered with the `-d`/`--test` mode that the fuzzer uses. The fuzzer harness may catch exceptions and exit cleanly, so a successful trigger should be confirmed by a sanitizer report of the OOB read rather than by a nonzero exit code.

title: Mach-O load-command iteration needs a remaining-bytes check before reading cmd/cmdsize
summary: The Mach-O header's ncmds drives load-command traversal; a truncated command region makes the first dereference of cmd/cmdsize read past the buffer.
content: A 32-bit Mach-O header has ncmds at offset 0x10 and sizeofcmds at offset 0x14, followed immediately by the load commands. Parsers commonly loop ncmds times and read the 8-byte (cmd, cmdsize) prefix at the current position before doing any length comparison. If the load-command region is shorter than 8 bytes but ncmds is non-zero, that prefix read is already out of bounds. The minimum unit to validate is the full load_command header, not just the presence of the header or the total sizeofcmds field.

title: LC_THREAD/LC_UNIXTHREAD cmdsize must cover flavor/count thread state
summary: Thread load commands in Mach-O contain register state; a cmdsize that only satisfies the generic 8-byte header lets PC extraction read past the command.
content: For LC_THREAD and LC_UNIXTHREAD, the command body is a list of (flavor, count) pairs followed by count 32-bit state words. The parser must validate that cmdsize covers the fixed thread_command header plus the state words described by the current flavor. A too-small cmdsize, or a count inconsistent with cmdsize, leaves the PC/saved-state read outside the validated bounds. When constructing Mach-O thread-command tests, shrink cmdsize and count independently from the architecture-specific state size to expose the gap.

title: Mach-O segment commands define file ranges that must be checked against the real file
summary: LC_SEGMENT fileoff/filesize pairs can point beyond the end of the input buffer; parsers that trust these fields in recovery paths read OOB.
content: A 32-bit LC_SEGMENT contains vmaddr, vmsize, fileoff, and filesize, followed by section data. The fileoff/filesize pair slices the on-disk buffer; if filesize is larger than the bytes remaining at fileoff, range computations produce an end pointer past the buffer. A minimal Mach-O with multiple segments can leave __LINKEDIT with a filesize that exceeds the actual file bytes, while the segment command itself remains structurally valid. When crafting Mach-O inputs, vary segment fileoff/filesize relative to the real file length, especially for file-backed segments like __LINKEDIT.

title: VQF header and chunk record layout
summary: VQF starts with 'TWIN97012000' and a big-endian header_size; chunks are tag+len+payload with big-endian lengths.
content: The VQF container is a 12-byte magic 'TWIN97012000' followed by a 4-byte big-endian header_size, then a sequence of chunks. Each chunk record is a 4-byte tag (read via little-endian I/O but representing a fourcc), a 4-byte big-endian length, and the payload. The demuxer's chunk walk is limited by the header_size countdown rather than the file size, so a chunk record near the end can declare more payload than is actually present.

title: VQF metadata short-read leaves uninitialized value
summary: VQF metadata handling ignores avio_read's return, so truncated metadata chunks cause uninitialized tail bytes to be treated as a string.
content: For recognized metadata chunks (for example NAME/META), VQF allocation is for the requested length plus one, then avio_read is expected to fill it, and the byte after the requested length is forcibly NUL-terminated. If EOF occurs before the requested length, the unfilled portion of the buffer is used as the metadata value. The value is not dereferenced immediately; the first strlen occurs later during metadata conversion, which is what the MemorySanitizer report points at.

title: VQF COMM mode validation gates the metadata path
summary: A valid COMM chunk with a supported rate/bitrate pair is needed before a metadata chunk will be processed.
content: The VQF header parser does not reach the metadata-chunk loop unless the COMM chunk passes mode validation. In this format family the COMM payload contains a channel count, a bitrate value, and a rate flag; the combination must map to a recognized audio mode (for example the 44/40 combination selects 44.1 kHz and a supported bitrate). A truncated or unsupported COMM causes the file to be rejected before the metadata handler is called.

title: VQF header_size budget controls metadata truncation
summary: Because add_metadata caps the read to the remaining header_size, a large declared metadata length combined with a small header budget yields a short read.
content: When a VQF metadata chunk is processed, the read length is the minimum of the chunk's declared length and the remaining header_size after the chunk header has been consumed. Therefore, keeping the preceding chunks small leaves a small budget, and a following metadata chunk with a much larger declared length will request exactly that budget and then hit EOF. This is the structural property that turns a normal VQF into an uninitialized-read trigger without needing a malformed length field.

title: WTV header and root directory pointer layout
summary: The WTV demuxer reads the root directory through a fixed header prefix: skip 0x30 bytes, then root size and root sector.
content: Before any chunks are parsed, the WTV demuxer validates a root directory. The controlling fields appear after a fixed 0x30-byte header: read root_size, skip 4 bytes, then read root_sector. The root_sector is a sector index rather than a byte offset, so the root directory table must be placed at root_sector * sector_size and its byte size must match root_size. If these fields do not lead to a valid table, read_header exits before any descriptor parsing is reached.

title: WTV directory entries are 24-byte records padded to 8 bytes
summary: WTV root-directory entries are variable length: a 24-byte base plus a name, with the entry padded to an 8-byte boundary.
content: Each WTV root-directory entry starts with a 24-byte field block, followed by a name whose length is stored in that block. The whole entry is padded up to an 8-byte boundary, and the demuxer advances by this padded size when walking the table. A synthetic WTV must reproduce this padding for every directory entry, including the final terminator, or the demuxer will read the table with the wrong stride.

title: WTV event and object GUIDs are stored in little-endian byte order
summary: WTV identifies events by 16-byte GUIDs in their on-disk little-endian order, so byte-order mistakes cause chunks to be ignored.
content: WTV stream events and media annotations are identified by 16-byte GUIDs. The demuxer compares the raw chunk GUID bytes against internal little-endian byte arrays, not against the canonical hyphenated string form. When constructing WTV files, convert a GUID into the exact little-endian byte layout; using network order or the canonical form directly will make the demuxer skip the chunk as unrecognized.

title: WTV chunk length bounds the descriptor copy buffer
summary: A WTV stream-description chunk's length field controls how many descriptor bytes are copied into the demuxer's finite buffer.
content: WTV timeline chunks are length-prefixed, and for stream-description events the payload is copied into an internal 258-byte stack buffer. The copied size is the minimum of the remaining chunk length and 258, so a chunk that ends immediately after a descriptor header leaves the parser at the boundary of initialized data. The original chunk length is what determines that boundary, so a minimal WTV should use a chunk length that exactly matches the descriptor bytes intended to be parsed.

title: MPEG-TS registration descriptor requires a 4-byte payload
summary: Descriptor tag 0x05 unconditionally reads 4 bytes even when its length byte says fewer, so an under-length 0x05 descriptor overruns.
content: The MPEG-TS descriptor list embedded in WTV uses the usual tag/length/value form. The generic parser accepts a descriptor as long as its declared length fits in the remaining descriptor-list bytes, but descriptor-specific parsing can still require more bytes than that length. For tag 0x05, the registration descriptor, the parser unconditionally reads a 4-byte format_identifier from the payload, so any length less than 4 overreads past the descriptor and can reach uninitialized memory. When generating descriptor lists, treat tag 0x05 as requiring a payload of at least 4 bytes.

title: WTV descriptor parsing needs a recognized stream-description event
summary: The descriptor parser runs only after a stream is created, so a WTV must include a stream-description event with a recognized mediatype.
content: The descriptor bytes that reach the MPEG-TS parser are nested inside a WTV stream-description event that also carries mediatype and subtype GUIDs. The demuxer does not parse the descriptor payload unless it first recognizes those GUIDs and creates an AVStream. A minimal WTV therefore needs the stream-description setup event with a known audio/video mediatype before any truncated descriptor chunk can be examined.

title: MVE signature length: ASCII phrase plus 0x1A 0x00 0x1A
summary: The Interplay MVE header magic is 21 bytes, not just the 18-byte ASCII phrase; the trailing control bytes are part of the signature read.
content: When constructing an Interplay MVE file (IPMOVIE), the demuxer checks a signature_buffer that starts with "Interplay MVE File" followed by the three bytes 0x1A 0x00 0x1A. The full signature is 21 bytes, and the header read requests 22 bytes because the buffer also has room for a NUL terminator. A file containing only the ASCII phrase is a truncated header: it will not pass normal probing, and in a forced demuxer path it leaves the trailing control bytes uninitialized before memcmp. Keep the trailing control bytes in any MVE sample meant to exercise the normal header path.

title: Truncated MVE header vs unchecked avio_read
summary: ipmovie_read_header memcmp's the entire signature buffer even when EOF makes avio_read return short; partial MVE headers trigger uninitialized reads.
content: The IPMOVIE header reader fetches the fixed signature into a stack buffer with avio_read and then memcmp's that buffer without checking the read count. A deliberately short MVE file whose length is between 1 and 21 bytes therefore does not stop at EOF: the uninitialized tail of the stack buffer is compared. This is a format-construction trap: complete MVE containers need the full 21-byte signature, but minimal truncated prefixes are the inputs that expose parser code assuming avio_read filled the requested buffer. In per-demuxer fuzzing where probing is bypassed, even an 18-byte ASCII prefix reaches this header parser, so short signature prefixes are the relevant construction shape for testing header validation.

title: MeshCoP timestamp/delay TLVs need fixed minimum length
summary: Under-length Active/Pending Timestamp and Delay Timer TLVs pass a selective validator but overrun later fixed-size reads.
content: The Thread MeshCoP Operational Dataset TLV is [type][length][value]. Active Timestamp (0x0e), Pending Timestamp (0x33), and Delay Timer (0x34) have fixed-size values: the timestamp values are 8 bytes and the delay timer is 4 bytes. If the length field is smaller than that fixed size, a validator that only enforces lengths for selected TLV types will still accept the record, while downstream parsing does a full-size value read. Undersizing these three TLV types is the format-level trigger for the out-of-bounds read.

title: Dataset validator default-accepts non-enumerated TLV types
summary: TLV types absent from the validator's explicit length checks fall through with zero minimum length.
content: MeshCoP Dataset validation is type-dependent: some TLV types have explicit minimum lengths, but every other type falls into a default case with no minimum. That default makes any non-enumerated TLV type a candidate for zero-length/under-length testing, because it will pass validation. When constructing focused malformed datasets, prefer TLV types outside the explicitly checked set unless the goal is to violate a checked field.

title: Buffer boundary placement for under-length TLVs
summary: A zero-length TLV at the end of the 254-byte Dataset moves the value read to the container boundary and turns under-length into OOB.
content: The Dataset TLV container is bounded to 254 bytes. For a zero-length TLV, the value pointer points just past the type and length bytes; if that TLV is the last record, the later fixed-size read can begin at or after the end of the backing buffer. Placement of the malformed TLV is therefore as important as the malformed length field when trying to make the over-read observable.

title: Filler TLVs must avoid explicitly validated types
summary: To reach the tail of a fixed-size Dataset, pad with zero-length default-accepted TLV types, not with length-checked network parameters.
content: Padding a Dataset TLV list to reach its tail requires filler records that the validator will accept. The safe fillers are zero-length TLVs whose types are not in the validator's explicit length-check cases; using channel, PAN ID, network-name, or security-policy fillers with invalid lengths would be rejected before reaching the malformed record. Keep the filler length field zero so each filler passes the default-valid path.

title: HDLC/Spinel framing vs CLI text for Dataset delivery
summary: The malformed Dataset TLV sequence must be wrapped in the harness's actual outer input format, often HDLC-framed Spinel rather than CLI hex.
content: The same MeshCoP Dataset bytes can be delivered through different outer formats: a CLI ASCII hex command, or an HDLC-framed Spinel property update. If the fuzz target is an NCP receive handler, the input is HDLC frames containing Spinel, and the Dataset TLV list is extracted from the Spinel payload before validation. Confirm the target's framing before constructing inputs; otherwise the malformed TLVs never reach the MeshCoP parser.

title: WASM table index space is import-shifted
summary: WASM table instructions index into a combined space of imported then defined tables, so a local table's index is shifted by the import count.
content: In the WASM binary format, table.get/table.set/table.grow/table.fill/table.copy immediates are LEB128 indices into a single table index space: imported tables occupy indices starting at 0, and module-defined tables follow them. A module with one imported table and one defined table must refer to the defined table as index 1, not 0. This import-count shift is the exact spot where loader-side table metadata lookup can go out of bounds. When constructing or fuzzing WASM modules, deliberately include a mix of imported and defined tables to exercise this resolution path.

title: WASM table-index validation fires during code-section parsing
summary: Table opcodes are validated while the loader parses the code section, so a bad table index crashes during load, not execution.
content: The code section (section id 10) contains function bodies, and each table instruction's index immediate is resolved during parsing for element-type validation. This means a malformed table index can produce an out-of-bounds read before the module is instantiated or any function is called. A load-time-only harness is therefore enough to observe the failure; no start function, export, or invocation is needed. The section ordering in the module still follows the normal WASM layout, but the vulnerable lookup is reached purely by the code-section bytes.

title: WASM bounds check and element-type lookup can use different index interpretations
summary: A table index that passes a combined-index bounds check can still be mis-resolved in the element-type lookup when imported and defined tables are mixed.
content: WASM loaders often perform two separate operations on a table instruction immediate: first check it against the total number of tables, then fetch the table's element type from a storage array. If these two code paths interpret the immediate differently (e.g. one treats it as the combined import+defined index while the other applies an import offset), the check can pass and the fetch still read out of bounds. The table section entry count and import section table count are both relevant; mismatches appear only when import_table_count is non-zero. Keep both values in mind when studying table-index handling in a WASM parser.

title: TIFF IFD entries must be written in ascending tag order
summary: libtiff silently drops unsorted IFD entries, so a minimal TIFF must sort its 12-byte tags by tag id.
content: A TIFF IFD is a 2-byte entry count followed by 12-byte entries (tag, type, count, value/offset) and a 4-byte next-IFD offset. libtiff warns on unsorted entries and ignores tags it cannot parse; missing ImageWidth or TileWidth then causes early rejection. When hand-building a TIFF, order every entry by ascending tag id (e.g. 256, 257, 258, ...) and put out-of-line data after the IFD. This is the first trap to check: an otherwise valid tiled JPEG TIFF can be rejected before any tile decompression if the IFD is not sorted.

title: Tiled JPEG TIFF required tags: Compression=7, TileWidth, TileLength, TileOffsets, TileByteCounts
summary: JPEG-compressed tiled TIFFs use TileWidth/TileLength instead of strip tags; Compression=7 selects the raw-tile JPEG path.
content: A tiled TIFF must define TileWidth (322) and TileLength (323), plus TileOffsets (273) and TileByteCounts (279), rather than StripOffsets/StripByteCounts. For JPEG tiles, Compression=7 with 8-bit samples and PhotometricInterpretation=2 (RGB) or 6 (YCbCr) is accepted by the tile decoder. TileWidth and TileLength are typically 16 or multiples of 16 for JPEG. With this tag set, the reader uses the raw tile read path instead of the simpler whole-image strip path.

title: TileByteCounts is authoritative; oversized counts make raw tile reads fail
summary: TIFF's raw tile read returns -1 when TileByteCounts exceeds available file data or tile offsets are invalid; this error may be ignored downstream.
content: TileOffsets and TileByteCounts are independent tags: libtiff does not verify until read time that the count fits in the file. An offset of 0 or a byte count extending past EOF makes TIFFReadRawTile return -1; a zero byte count can make it return 0. Because TIFF has no per-tile checksum, the decoder learns the tile is bad only from the read return value. Crafting a tile entry with an inconsistent offset/count pair is a reliable way to reach the error path in the tile decompression code.

title: Raw-tile read returns are signed; zero/negative sizes must be checked
summary: A negative TIFF tile read size stored in an unsigned variable becomes a huge length and is passed to the JPEG decompressor as the input length.
content: The raw tile API returns a signed count: -1 for I/O failure, 0 for an empty tile, and a positive byte count on success. If the reader stores that in an unsigned type, -1 becomes SIZE_MAX and the JPEG source manager is told its input buffer is that large. The marker scan then continues far beyond the actual tile buffer and reads out of bounds. The container-level lesson is that a TileByteCounts value which fails the raw read is not caught by TIFF's own structure; the decoder must re-check the signed return before decompressing.

title: JPEG tile decoding uses TIFFTileSize-derived buffers, not the tile byte count
summary: The compressed buffer is sized from tile geometry and sample layout, while TileByteCounts controls the raw read length; the mismatch is a construction trap.
content: For tiled JPEG TIFFs, the compressed tile buffer is often allocated as twice the TIFFTileSize computed from TileWidth, TileLength, BitsPerSample, and SamplesPerPixel. TileByteCounts tells libtiff how many bytes to read into that buffer. If TileByteCounts is inconsistent with the file's actual tile payload, the raw read fails before decompression, but the logical tile geometry still controls the allocated buffer size. A small 16x16 8-bit RGB tile with an inconsistent large TileByteCounts can therefore make the JPEG marker scanner walk past the end of a small heap buffer.

title: TIFF byte-order header and IFD offsets
summary: A hand-built TIFF needs the correct II/MM magic, magic 42, and an IFD offset; a bad offset causes rejection before tag parsing.
content: A TIFF begins with a 2-byte byte-order mark (II for little-endian or MM for big-endian), then 2-byte magic 42, then a 4-byte offset to the first IFD. The IFD must be located exactly at that offset and be complete before any out-of-line arrays referenced by its entries. If the offset points to 0 or into an unrelated structure, libtiff rejects the file before tile tags are parsed. This header layout is the prerequisite for all tiled-JPEG construction experiments.

title: TIFF IFD inline width and zero value_offset trap
summary: Classic TIFF IFD entries hold values inline only when size <= 4 (BigTIFF: 8); oversize entries with value_offset=0 are not inline data.
content: A TIFF directory entry stores either an inline value or an offset to a value, and the parser decides by comparing type_size * count against the inline capacity (4 for classic TIFF, 8 for BigTIFF). If the computed size exceeds that capacity, the entry must point out-of-line to a real file location. Offset 0 is not a valid out-of-line location because it overlaps the TIFF header, so a lenient parser that treats it as 'inline' ends up reading count*type_size bytes from the small inline union.

title: Tag count multiplies the out-of-bounds read from an inline union
