summary: In an IFD entry, the count field controls how many bytes are read; a large count with a zero offset turns a small inline union into a long OOB read.
content: When value_offset is zero, the parser constructs the returned vector/string directly from the inline storage pointer. The length is tag.count multiplied by dataTypeSize, not bounded by the inline buffer size. For example, an ASCII tag with a byte count much larger than the inline capacity will be read as if those bytes were contiguous in the IFD entry, crossing into adjacent struct fields and past the struct boundary. The practical format lesson is to validate count*dataTypeSize against the inline capacity before choosing the inline path.

title: TIFF ASCII tags follow the same vector/offset rule as numeric tags
summary: ASCII and other string/array tags are parsed with identical inline/out-of-line logic; a zero out-of-line offset can expose an ASCII buffer as incomplete inline bytes.
content: In TIFF, string tags are stored as tag type + count, just like numeric arrays, and the inline threshold applies to the raw byte length. If an ASCII tag has a byte count that forces it out-of-line but its offset is zero, the parser treats the inline union as the initial part of the string and then reads past it. This matters because such strings are often passed to higher-level code such as filenames, SRS text, or application keys before validation. Constructors should remember that for ASCII tags the count is in bytes, so a short count can still cross the inline threshold.

title: TIFF parser dispatch: make the strict parser reject before the fallback opens
summary: A malformed TIFF can be routed to a second parser by making a required semantic element invalid for the first parser while still acceptable to the second.
content: TIFF parsing often has multiple registered parsers; the first one that accepts the file wins. The file must therefore fail the strict parser's required-feature check but still be considered openable by the fallback parser. One structural example is a palette TIFF (PhotometricInterpretation=3) that references a ColorMap but does not provide it: the strict parser rejects the missing directory item, and the fallback parser proceeds. The construction trap is to confirm which parser actually opens the file and to test the fallback in isolation.

title: Contiguous binary member bytes in a virtual tar input
summary: When the input to a TIFF fuzzer is an in-memory archive of members, the TIFF member's bytes must be contiguous after the archive member header; line-wrapping corrupts all file offsets.
content: Archive-style harnesses usually extract named members and parse their content as files. The member content starts immediately after the member header line and runs until the next member marker, so any inserted newline or textual representation shifts the extracted bytes. For a TIFF this is fatal because the parser relies on absolute file offsets from the header through the IFD to out-of-line tag data. When hand-building such an archive, keep the TIFF member as one exact binary blob rather than splitting it into ASCII lines.

title: BTF.ext header field layout and hdr_len semantics
summary: The BTF.ext container starts with a 32-byte header; core_relo_off/core_relo_len are the last fields at offsets 24 and 28.
content: The BTF.ext section begins with a fixed 32-byte header: u16 magic, u8 version, u8 flags, u32 hdr_len, u32 func_info_off, u32 func_info_len, u32 line_info_off, u32 line_info_len, u32 core_relo_off, u32 core_relo_len. The core_relo_off and core_relo_len fields are located at byte offsets 24 and 28. hdr_len is self-reported: values smaller than 32 normally mean the core_relo fields are logically absent, but those fields still occupy the same offsets and can be read before any size validation is performed.

title: Truncated BTF.ext header before core_relo fields
summary: Set hdr_len=24 and keep the .BTF.ext section size between 25 and 31 bytes so core_relo_off/len are read outside the section.
content: A useful construction trick is to give the BTF.ext header hdr_len=24, which is enough for func_info and line_info metadata, but make the actual ELF section only 25-31 bytes long. The parser initializes core_relo_off and core_relo_len from offsets 24 and 28 before checking whether hdr_len covers them. This ordering causes an out-of-bounds read past the declared section boundary. Keep func_info_len and line_info_len zero so the parser proceeds past the earlier fields.

title: ELF section sh_size defines the BTF.ext boundary
summary: For malformed BTF.ext inputs, the usable data length is the ELF section's sh_size, not the whole file size.
content: When crafting an ELF carrying .BTF.ext, the loader treats the section's sh_size as the amount of data available to the BTF.ext parser. To create a truncated header, set sh_size to a value between 25 and 31 while placing hdr_len=24 inside the section content. The section content can be shorter than the full 32-byte BTF.ext header; the ELF section header is the boundary that determines where the over-read starts.

title: ELF container constraints for BPF object loading
summary: The raw ELF must be 64-bit little-endian ET_REL with e_machine 0 or EM_BPF and a valid section/symbol table.
content: The BPF object loader expects an ELF64 little-endian relocatable object of type ET_REL, with e_machine set to 0 or EM_BPF, and requires a proper section header table and symbol table. BTF and BTF.ext sections must be present as PROGBITS sections. If these ELF-level structural requirements are not satisfied, the loader aborts before reaching the BTF-specific parsing logic.

title: Dependency of .BTF.ext on a valid .BTF section
summary: A malformed .BTF.ext is only reached if a minimal valid .BTF section is also present and accepted.
content: The .BTF.ext section is processed as a companion to an already-valid .BTF section. A minimal accepted .BTF section consists of the 24-byte BTF header: magic 0xeb9f, version 1, flags 0, hdr_len=24, and type_off/type_len/str_off/str_len all zero. If .BTF is missing or fails that header validation, the loader skips .BTF.ext entirely, so any BTF.ext-focused input must include this minimal valid .BTF section to reach the vulnerable code path.

title: MD3 header field validation is per-offset, not global
summary: MD3 exposes OFS_FRAMES/OFS_TAGS/OFS_SURFACES/OFS_EOF; only some are range-checked before use.
content: The MD3 header is 108 bytes and contains separate offsets for frames, tags, surfaces, and EOF. In the vulnerable importer, validation covered OFS_FRAMES, OFS_SURFACES, and OFS_EOF but omitted OFS_TAGS. That asymmetry means a format builder can keep every checked offset valid while setting the unchecked tag offset to an arbitrary value. When constructing MD3 test files, treat every OFS_* field as an independently attacker-controlled pointer and verify each against fileSize before the parser dereferences it.

title: MD3 tag records are fixed-size with a leading C-string field
summary: MD3 tag parsing trusts NUM_TAGS and reads a 64-byte NAME field, so truncated tags can drive OOB strlen.
content: Each MD3 tag is a fixed-size record: a 64-byte NAME field, a vec3 origin, and a 3x3 axis matrix, totaling 112 bytes. The tag loop reads pcTags->NAME and treats it as a NUL-terminated string, so a record whose bytes are not entirely within the file can cause strlen to run past the buffer. NUM_TAGS is also untrusted, so a few in-bounds tags followed by a truncated tag are enough to trigger repeated out-of-bounds reads.

title: Minimum MD3 surface is one 108-byte surface header plus one triangle/vertex
summary: A single non-empty surface satisfies MD3 surface validation and lets tests focus on header offsets.
content: The MD3 surface structure has its own 108-byte header containing counts and OFS_TRIS, OFS_SHADERS, OFS_ST, OFS_XYZNORMAL, and OFS_END. To reach tag processing, only one valid non-empty surface is required, e.g. one triangle and one vertex, with sub-offsets pointing to immediately following data. Keeping the surface minimal is useful for format fuzzing because it reduces unrelated mesh-processing code paths.

title: TFTP request opcode and NUL-terminated strings
summary: TFTP RRQ/WRQ is a 2-byte opcode followed by filename and mode, each NUL-terminated; the Request unit completes at the mode NUL.
content: TFTP's read/write request uses network-order opcodes 1 (RRQ) and 2 (WRQ). The rest of the packet is filename then mode, both NUL-terminated strings. There is no overall length or checksum, so the parser depends entirely on the two NUL bytes to know where the unit ends. On little-endian hosts, the wire opcode for RRQ is bytes 00 01, not 01 00.

title: TFTP opcode 3/4 paths do not hit the Request completion hook
summary: In TFTP, the end-of-unit hook is tied to parsing a Request, not to every valid TFTP packet; use a single RRQ/WRQ to exercise it.
content: TFTP has five opcodes: RRQ=1, WRQ=2, DATA=3, ACK=4, ERROR=5. The generated parser selects the unit type by opcode; only RRQ/WRQ parse variable-length strings and end with a 'request' unit completion. DATA/ACK have short fixed fields and are not the path that invokes the request-unit end-of-message action, so a successful transfer simulation is unnecessary. A single well-formed request packet is the smallest message that reaches that action.

title: Uninitialized callback pointer remains hidden until a unit completes
summary: If parser runtime stores completion callbacks in uninitialized pointer members, any valid TFTP Request completion reads them; test with the shortest request that reaches that completion.
content: When a parser runtime object has an empty user-defined constructor, raw function-pointer members are not zero-initialized, so their values are undefined. A Request unit in TFTP completes immediately after the mode's NUL, before any TFTP state machine is built. This makes a minimal RRQ/WRQ the natural probe for an uninitialized completion-callback read; no DATA/ACK exchange, retransmission, or transfer-state setup is needed.

title: JPEG-R dual-image container: primary JPEG + appended gainmap JPEG
summary: A JPEG-R image is two concatenated JPEGs; the parser finds the gainmap by scanning for the next SOI marker.
content: JPEG-R is structurally a normal primary JPEG followed by a secondary gain-map JPEG. The parser scans the byte stream for the 0xFFD8 (SOI) marker of the second image, so no external index is required: a valid dual-image file can be formed by concatenating a complete primary JPEG, the 0xFFD8 marker, and a complete secondary JPEG. The secondary image should encode the gain map and is commonly grayscale. A single JPEG truncated after an APP2 segment will not reach the metadata layer because the container split and JPEG validity checks happen first.

title: ISO gain-map metadata APP2 segment: namespace + metadata
summary: Gain-map metadata is carried in an APP2 (0xFFE2) segment of the gain-map JPEG, starting with a fixed namespace string.
content: The ISO 21496-1 gain-map metadata segment starts with the fixed namespace 'urn:iso:std:iso:ts:21496:-1' followed by a NUL, and only the bytes after that namespace are parsed as the actual metadata. In the JPEG APP2 segment, the 16-bit length field is big-endian and counts the length bytes themselves plus the payload, so the payload length in the segment is the field value minus 2. A parser that trusts this declared size but subtracts the namespace length to build its working vector ends up with exactly 'declared payload length - namespace length' metadata bytes.

title: Unsigned length arithmetic underflow in metadata parsing
summary: A bounds check like pos >= data.size() - N silently passes when data.size() < N because size_t subtraction wraps.
content: When the working metadata vector is shorter than the width needed by the next read, an unsigned subtraction such as data.size() - 3 wraps to a huge value and the bounds check no longer guards the read. For the ISO gain-map metadata, a vector of exactly two bytes passes the two single-byte reads and then reaches a 4-byte read whose size-minus-3 bound underflows. This is a concrete construction trap: the metadata payload after the namespace must be shorter than 4 bytes, while still being long enough for the leading single-byte fields.

title: Metadata field order determines viable truncation lengths
summary: The parser consumes a version byte and a flags byte before the underflowing 4-byte read, so truncating to two payload bytes is the shortest path to the faulty read.
content: The ISO gain-map metadata begins with a one-byte version and a one-byte flags field, followed by 32-bit fields. If the metadata vector after the namespace is one byte, parsing fails on the flags read; with two bytes, both single-byte reads succeed and the next 4-byte read uses the underflowed size check. The values of those first two bytes are not critical for reaching the underflow because the parser does not reject them before the 4-byte read.

title: JPEG-R validation constraints: primary color space and gainmap dimensions
summary: The decoder validates basic image properties before parsing metadata, so the constructed primary/gainmap pair must meet those checks.
content: The JPEG-R decoder enforces basic JPEG properties before parsing gain-map metadata: the primary image must be a valid YCbCr 4:2:0 JPEG and the gainmap must be a second valid JPEG, typically grayscale. Dimensions are also checked against limits, but the gainmap dimensions can derive from the primary via scale factors. A small valid primary with a same-size grayscale gainmap is enough to pass the image-format validation and reach the later metadata parsing path.
